title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 307: The Evolution of Altruism
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 307 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Evolution of Altruism: Beyond the Selfish Gene

Paragraph 1. For almost fifty years, biology was dominated by a harsh viewpoint: living creatures are biological machines built to pass on their own genetic material at any cost. Made famous by Richard Dawkins in his 1976 book The Selfish Gene, this model treated apparent kindness in nature as hidden selfishness. Helping others was explained either through 'kin selection'—protecting relatives who share your genes—or through returning favours later. Traditional biologists viewed pure sacrifice for an unrelated stranger as impossible under evolution.

Paragraph 2. In Mutual Aid: The Science of Cooperation, evolutionary scientist Dr. Marcus Sterling challenges that cynical belief. Sterling does not deny that genetic self-interest works at small individual levels, but argues scientists ignored group survival. Across thousands of species, from underground mole-rats to ocean whales, united teams consistently outperform selfish loners. A tribe of early humans willing to share food and risk danger to protect the group will naturally defeat a divided group of selfish individuals.

Paragraph 3. Sterling supports his argument using game theory, especially the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. Computer simulations built by political scientist Robert Axelrod proved that in repeated rounds, purely aggressive players who cheat partners always suffer terrible collapse. By contrast, cooperative rules like 'tit-for-tat'—starting kindly and then copying a partner's last move—produce steady long-term stability. Sterling adds that human brains evolved chemical rewards: sharing with others releases oxytocin and dopamine, showing we are biologically built for solidarity.

Paragraph 4. In his final chapters, Sterling criticizes modern economic systems. He argues that schools, workplaces, and public policies wrongly assume humans are purely selfish individuals trying only to maximize personal gain, which quietly weakens our natural habit of mutual aid. Although human history contains violence, Sterling shows our species survived not through the victory of the strongest single fighter, but through trust, cooperation, and care for the vulnerable.

groups.title: Questions 1–5
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

q1.text: Richard Dawkins wrote The Selfish Gene after studying whales for ten years.

steps: Đoạn 1: Chỉ nhắc Dawkins viết sách năm 1976, không hề nhắc ông nghiên cứu cá voi 10 năm.
Kết luận: NOT GIVEN.

q2.text: Traditional biologists doubted that animals would sacrifice themselves for unrelated strangers.

steps: Đoạn 1: "Traditional biologists viewed pure sacrifice for an unrelated stranger as impossible..."
Kết luận: TRUE.

q3.text: Dr. Marcus Sterling claims that genetic self-interest does not exist at all in nature.

steps: Đoạn 2: "Sterling does not deny that genetic self-interest works at small individual levels..."
Kết luận: FALSE.

q4.text: In repeated computer games, cooperative 'tit-for-tat' rules create steady long-term stability.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...cooperative rules like 'tit-for-tat'... produce steady long-term stability."
Kết luận: TRUE.

q5.text: Human survival depended mainly on the physical strength of single violent fighters.

steps: Đoạn 4: Loài người tồn tại nhờ tin tưởng và hợp tác, không phải chiến thắng của cá nhân mạnh nhất.
Kết luận: FALSE.

q6.text: What does 'kin selection' mean in the first paragraph?
options: A. Fighting rival tribes for territory
B. Trading food with strangers for profit
C. Copying the behaviour of aggressive animals
D. Protecting family members who share the same genes

steps: Đoạn 1: "'kin selection'—protecting relatives who share your genes."
Kết luận: Chọn D.

q7.text: Why does Sterling mention early human tribes in the second paragraph?
options: A. To prove early humans never experienced conflict
B. To show that cooperative groups outlast selfish ones
C. To explain why whales live in large oceans
D. To argue that individual hunting was always best

steps: Đoạn 2: Bộ lạc biết chia sẻ và bảo vệ nhau sẽ đánh bại nhóm ích kỷ chia rẽ.
Kết luận: Chọn B.

q8.text: What happened to purely selfish strategies in Robert Axelrod's computer tests?
options: A. They collapsed over repeated rounds.
B. They defeated every cooperative player.
C. They worked only during the final round.
D. They turned slowly into 'tit-for-tat' rules.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...purely aggressive players who cheat partners always suffer terrible collapse."
Kết luận: Chọn A.

q9.text: Why does Sterling discuss oxytocin and dopamine?
options: A. To warn against taking medical pills
B. To show how stress damages memory
C. To prove human brains physically reward sharing
D. To explain why people dislike working in offices

steps: Đoạn 3: Não tiết hormone hưng phấn khi chia sẻ chứng tỏ con người có cơ chế sinh học hướng về đoàn kết.
Kết luận: Chọn C.

q10.text: What flaw does Sterling identify in modern economic institutions?
options: A. They spend too much money on wildlife research.
B. They treat humans as purely selfish and weaken teamwork.
C. They prevent students from attending university.
D. They reward lazy workers more than hardworking ones.

steps: Đoạn 4: Mặc định con người chỉ tối đa hóa lợi ích cá nhân làm suy yếu bản năng tương trợ.
Kết luận: Chọn B.
